mapped_topics.label: Geometrical interpretation and applications of Rolle’s theorem

blocks.text: If f is continuous on \([a,b]\), differentiable on \((a,b)\), and \(f(a)=f(b)\), then \(f\prime(c)=0\) for at least one \(c\in(a,b)\).
Geometrically the endpoints have the same height, and an interior tangent is parallel to the x-axis.

blocks.alt: Rolle’s theorem: equal-height endpoints and an interior horizontal tangent
blocks.caption: Rolle’s theorem: equal-height endpoints and an interior horizontal tangent — ROS: unchanged source crop.

blocks.text: Polynomials, sine, cosine and exponentials are continuous on the real line. Tangent is discontinuous at its poles; \(\log x\) requires \(x>0\). Check the domain before the theorem.

items.title: Polynomial on [−2,3]
paragraphs: Being a polynomial, f is continuous on the closed interval and differentiable in its interior. Also \(f(-2)=0=f(3)\).
The endpoint roots do not belong to the open interval. The interior root is \(6c+2=0\), giving \(c=-1/3\in(-2,3)\).

items.title: When Rolle’s theorem cannot be applied
question_paragraphs: Explain why Rolle’s theorem does not apply to (i) \(\tan x\) on \([0,\pi]\), (ii) \(1/x^2\) on \([-1,1]\), and (iii) \(x^3\) on \([1,3]\).
paragraphs: (i) Although the endpoints agree, \(\tan x\) is undefined at \(\pi/2\), so continuity fails.
(ii) The function is undefined at zero, so continuity on the closed interval fails.
(iii) The polynomial is continuous and differentiable, but \(f(1)=1\ne27=f(3)\).
items.final_answer: Each example violates a required hypothesis.
